fields.meta_title: Favorite Things Questionnaire for Gift Giving | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a favorite things questionnaire for teachers, coworkers, or a party, and send the answers to whoever buys the gift. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Favorite Things Questionnaire for Whoever Buys the Gift
fields.hero_description: Build a favorite things questionnaire that gets each person's answers to their gift buyer and keeps them in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Happens After Someone Fills It In
fields.features_subheading: A favorite things questionnaire records what a person likes before someone shops for them. Emergent builds what comes after.
fields.feature_1:
Questions written from a plain description

Describe who answers and who shops, such as teachers and the parents buying for them. Emergent builds the questions and their database, then changes either one on request.
fields.feature_2:
One question per screen on a phone

A teacher can answer between classes when the questionnaire shows one question per screen. Short fields for a coffee order sit next to longer ones for hobbies and favorite stores.
fields.feature_3:
Every questionnaire saved as a row you own

Each completed questionnaire becomes a row in a database you own, with a column per question. Sort by birthday month, filter out nut allergies, or find everyone who named one store.
fields.feature_4:
Reminders tied to the dates in the answers

Set a reminder against any date a person gives you, such as a birthday or a work anniversary. The app sends it by Slack or email, with that person's favorites inside the message.
fields.feature_5:
No cap on how many people answer

Send it to a class of 25 or a company of 900. Emergent puts no response caps on forms. People who answer the night before a holiday party still land in the same database.
fields.feature_6:
Code that moves to your own repository

On paid plans, export the full code to your GitHub repository. A PTA or an HR team can hand the questionnaire to its own developer and keep building on it outside Emergent.

fields.tab_content_1:
Parents pull up any teacher's favorites in the PTA directory

Larkspur Elementary's PTA sends the questionnaire to teachers in September, and 28 of its 31 teachers have answered. Parents search the PTA directory by name. Ms. Nakashima's entry shows an iced oat milk latte, salted dark chocolate, and a note that she avoids nuts.
fields.tab_content_2:
7 days before a birthday, the favorites reach the manager

Renata Ilves runs the office at Brookhaven Freight, where all 46 employees answered when they started. The app sends her a Slack direct message 7 days before each birthday. For Theo Marchand's birthday on March 14, the message lists sour gummies, a Thai place on Elm Street, and trail running.
fields.tab_content_3:
Hand cream goes to whoever claims it first

Margo Pennington caps every item at $15 for her favorite things party, and each of her 12 guests brings 3 of one item they love. The questionnaire asks for that item first. When Imani Rhodes typed lavender hand cream, the form showed that Celia Ward had already claimed it. Imani picked a citrus candle instead.
fields.tab_content_4:
Each giver sees one coworker's answers

Saltmarsh Design draws names in December for a gift exchange with 18 people and a $30 limit. Everyone answers the questionnaire first. The app then emails each giver the answers of the one coworker they drew. Jonah Wexley drew Lena Sato: green tea, mystery novels, and anything for her bike.

fields.howto_title: How to Make a Favorite Things Questionnaire
fields.howto_description: These seven steps create a favorite things questionnaire whose answers reach the person buying the gift, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Decide who will read the answers
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask for things a person can buy
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Make room for allergies and dislikes
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide who reads the answers before you write a single question. Parents buying for a teacher need a coffee order and any allergies. An office manager planning birthdays needs the date. Party guests need to know which items are already taken.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Ask about things someone can buy or book: a coffee order, a snack, a store, a restaurant, a hobby. Leave out questions like a favorite season unless you plan to shop for it. Keep the list short enough to finish on a phone.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Add one field for allergies and one for gifts the person does not want, such as scented candles or another mug. A careful gift buyer reads these first. Mark both optional, since some people would rather not say.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Pick where answers land and who can read them. A PTA directory can show every teacher's entry to every parent. A gift exchange should let each giver read only the person they drew, with everyone else's answers kept private.
fields.howto_step_5_des: If the questionnaire asks for a birthday or a start date, attach a reminder to it. Choose how far ahead it arrives, such as 7 days, and whether it goes to Slack or email, with the person's favorites in the message.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Describe the questionnaire to Emergent in plain English: who answers, which questions, where the answers go, and when reminders fire. Emergent builds the form and the database behind it. Ask for changes the same way, such as a new question about bookstores.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Send it to two people first
fields.howto_step_7_des: Try it with two testers and read their answers as the gift buyer would. Rewrite any question that came back vague, such as snacks with no flavor or brand. Then send it to the whole class or the whole office.

faq_plan.q: What are your favorite things questionnaire?
faq_plan.ref: What are your favorite things questionnaire?

prov.original: What are your favorite things questionnaire?

faq_plan.a: A favorite things questionnaire asks one person a short set of questions about what they like, such as a coffee order, snacks, stores, and hobbies. A PTA sends it to teachers, an office manager to employees, and a party host to guests, and the answers tell the gift buyer what to get.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a favorite things questionnaire?
faq_plan.a: Describe it to Emergent's AI form builder in plain English, naming who answers, what to ask, and who reads the answers. Emergent builds the questionnaire and a database for the answers, and adds reminders or a lookup page when you ask. The free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: What is a good list of questions for a favorite things questionnaire?
faq_plan.a: A good list asks for things a gift buyer can act on: a drink order, snacks, stores, restaurants, hobbies, colors, and books or music. Add a question for allergies and another for gifts to avoid. Keep it to 10 to 15 questions so it can be finished on a phone.

faq_plan.q: What should a teacher favorite things questionnaire ask?
faq_plan.a: It should ask for what a parent can buy: the teacher's coffee or tea order, favorite snacks, stores for gift cards, the classroom supplies that run out first, and any allergies. Questions about how the class is going belong on a separate feedback form. Send the favorite things questionnaire for teachers early in the school year, and families have it before the holidays.

faq_plan.q: What goes on a favorite things party questionnaire?
faq_plan.a: It asks each guest which item they will bring, confirms the item fits the host's price limit, and checks it against what other guests already claimed. Add a few questions about each guest's own favorites, and the host can share those on the day. Emergent builds the claim check from the same plain-English description as the rest of the form.

faq_plan.q: How do I roll out a favorite things questionnaire for employees?
faq_plan.a: Send it during onboarding, while a new hire is already filling in forms, then once a year to everyone so answers stay current. Ask for a birthday or work anniversary if you want reminders tied to those dates. Forms built with Emergent carry no response caps, and the yearly refresh can go to all employees at once.

faq_plan.q: Should a staff favorite things questionnaire be optional?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Make every question optional and say at the top who will see the answers. Some staff would rather not share a birthday or an allergy, and a skipped question should not hold up the rest. Keep it apart from any assessment form, and never let the answers feed into a review.

faq_plan.q: Who should see the answers on an employee favorite things questionnaire?
faq_plan.a: Only the people buying gifts should see them: an office manager, an HR lead, or the coworker who drew a name. Everyone else sees their own answers and nothing more. In an app Emergent builds, the answers live in a database you own, and you decide which page shows which rows.

faq_plan.q: How do I keep a favorite things questionnaire up to date?
faq_plan.a: Send each person a link that opens their existing answers for editing, and ask everyone to review them once a year. Show the date each answer was last changed. A gift buyer can then tell a coffee order from 4 years ago apart from one given last month.

faq_plan.q: Can a favorite things questionnaire be part of new hire paperwork?
faq_plan.a: Yes, as a separate, optional step after the required forms. Put it after the employee information form, which holds the details payroll and HR need, and let a new hire skip it without holding anything up. Keep the birthday question optional as well.

plan.angle: The top 10 for favorite things questionnaire is printables, Etsy and Pinterest templates and one Typeform gifting post: a sheet of blanks someone fills in once and a parent or office manager loses track of. None of them shows what happens after the answers come in. This page shows the questionnaire as a small app for four real gift-giving jobs: a PTA that lets parents look up each teacher, an office manager who gets an employee's favorites before a birthday, a favorite things party host who stops duplicate items, and a gift exchange that sends each giver only one person's answers. The FAQ covers the questions to ask, teacher, staff and employee versions, and the party format.
